label: Claude Sonnet 5.5
output:
Here's the letter. Put your name at the bottom. Since the open evening is eight days away, I'd post it first class tomorrow so it lands in time.

---

Peckham
11 November 2026

Kelechi,

You said put it in writing, so here it is, in writing, with a stamp and everything. I hope the postman in Croydon gave you a funny look. I hope you're on the train right now, a bit squashed, reading this instead of looking at your phone like everybody else.

I'm going to try not to preach, because I know you. The moment someone starts a sermon your face goes blank and you start thinking about lunch. So I'll tell you a few things that happened, a few things I think, and then ask you for one small thing.

You were moaning at my birthday, and I let you, because it was my birthday and you were buying drinks. But it wasn't new. Nine years, and every day is the same spreadsheet. You've said it so many times I could write your costings for you. And last year on your own birthday, when you'd had a drink and got honest, you said you just wanted to do something that matters before 40. I haven't forgotten that. I don't think you have either.

So here is my case. Teach maths.

I know. You laughed. Keep reading.

Remember Moremi, before exams? Half the hostel was outside your door with exercise books. People who had barely opened a textbook all semester were sitting on the floor while you explained things, and somehow they left understanding it. You got an A in further maths and you never once made anyone feel stupid for not having one. That is not a small thing, Kelechi. Most people who are good at maths are terrible at explaining it, because they've forgotten what it's like not to see it. You haven't. You can still remember what it's like to be lost, and that's the whole job.

At Christmas you sat my nephew down with fractions, and the boy was going nowhere with the textbook. You grabbed plates and started dividing jollof rice into portions. He still talks about it. He told me last month, unprompted, that "Uncle Kelechi's rice maths" was the first time fractions made sense. You didn't even know you were teaching. You were just being yourself with a plate of food. Now imagine that, with a proper plan, in front of a class that actually needs it.

Let me tell you about Damola. He's in Year 11 and he'd been stuck on simultaneous equations for three weeks. Three weeks of him looking at me like I was speaking another language, and me trying every angle I could think of. Then last month it clicked, and he shouted "Is that all??" in front of everyone. The whole class clapped. Some of them don't even like maths. They just knew what it had cost him. I had to turn round and pretend to find something on the board because my eyes had gone.

That moment doesn't happen on a spreadsheet. I don't want to be dramatic about it, but nobody has ever clapped for a corrected costing.

Now the honest part, because you wouldn't believe me otherwise and you'd be right not to.

Teaching is hard. Properly hard. The marking never ends. You finish a set and there's another set. Some days the behaviour is wahala, and you'll go home wondering what you're doing with your life. When I started in 2019 I cried in the car park twice in my first term. Twice. I'm telling you because I'm not hiding it, and because it did get better. It gets better the way anything does when you keep showing up. You learn the tricks, you find your voice, the kids learn who you are. But it doesn't start easy and I'm not going to pretend it does.

The money is the other thing, and I won't dodge it. The first year, your pay drops. You know that already, and it's a real consideration, not something to wave away. But you're a quantity surveyor. Sit down and cost it. Do your own numbers properly: the first-year drop, then the holidays, the pension, and the pay going up after. You do this for strangers every day for a living, so do it for yourself once and see what you get. If the sums say no, fine, then at least you'll know. I just think you've never run them because the answer might be inconvenient.

And you're not too old. You're 34. A woman in my department started at 41 and she is one of the best teachers we have. Nobody walks into a classroom at 22 knowing what they're doing anyway. The ones who come in later bring something the kids can feel, which is that they chose it.

There's also a practical thing. Our school has 1,100 kids, and since September two of our Year 9 maths groups have been covered by a supply teacher. That's not a disaster, but it's not what those kids should have, and it's the same story in a lot of schools. They need people who can actually do this. You are wasting yourself checking other people's costings. I mean that kindly, but I mean it.

Now the ask, and it's small.

The salaried route is the one I think suits you, where you get paid while you train. It's one year, and it starts September 2027, with applications opening soon. There's an open evening this Thursday week, 19 November, at 6pm, at the training partnership in Lewisham. All I'm asking is that you come. You don't have to sign anything. You don't have to decide anything. Just go and look at it, ask your questions, and be rude about the biscuits if you want. I'll come with you. I'll even buy food after, so at worst you get a free meal and an evening of me being insufferable.

If you go and it feels wrong, you'll have lost one evening and I'll never mention it again. Well, I'll mention it once. But if you go and something in you wakes up a bit, then you'll have found out something nine years of spreadsheets couldn't tell you.

You said if I was serious I should put it in writing. I'm serious. This is the most serious thing I've written since my PGCE, and I had to look up how to address an envelope.

Reply to me by voice note, obviously, because you're a hypocrite. But reply.

Your guy always,

[Your name]

P.S. I've told no one else about this letter, so if you ignore it, only the two of us will know. And Damola, because he asks about everything.

---

I'd double-check two things before printing. The P.S. about Damola is a joke I invented, so cut it if it doesn't sound like you. I also wrote that your nephew told you recently about the "rice maths" and called Kelechi "Uncle Kelechi", which wasn't in your notes, so change or remove that if it isn't true. I left out any pay figures since I don't know them, and the "I'll buy food after" is an offer I added on your behalf, so keep it only if you mean it.
